title: Euclid XI.Def.6-8: The inclination of a plane to a plane is the acute angle contained by the straight lines drawn at right angles to the intersection at the same point…
summary: Euclid XI.Def.6-8: The inclination of a plane to a plane is the acute angle contained by the straight lines drawn at right angles to the intersection at the same point…
body: Euclid, Book XI, XI.Def.6-8, as worded on this page: "The inclination of a plane to a plane is the acute angle contained by the straight lines drawn at right angles to the intersection at the same point, one in each of the planes. A plane is said to be similarly inclined to a plane as another is to another when the said angles of the inclinations equal one another. Parallel planes are those which do not meet." The argument printed under that statement begins: "Definition 6 Definition 7 Definition 8 Guide As the previous definition requires certain assumptions, so does definition 6. It assumes that any two such acute angles are equal, something Euclid does not prove but could have in the course of Book XI. Definition 8 is analogous to definition I.23 for parallel lines in a plane. There is no proposition in Book XI which states that parallelism of planes is a transitive relation, but that is not difficult to prove given the rest of the propositions in the book. The first appearance of parallel planes is in proposition XI.14 . When two planes are not parallel, then, by this definition, they intersect. Proposition XI.3 proclaims that this…" The page is David E. Joyce's text of the Elements. He describes that text as similar to Heath's translation of Heiberg, and slightly less literal.
said_by: Euclid, in David E. Joyce's text of the Elements at Clark University
